US July PPI year over year fell to 2.2%, core flat month over month

The latest producer price data released by the U.S. Department of Labor showed that July’s overall PPI came in weaker than market expectations, with upstream inflation pressures continuing to ease. Market participants see it as one of the key clues for observing the Federal Reserve’s policy path, and attention quickly shifted to the subsequent, more heavily weighted consumer price data.

On the core facts, July PPI rose 2.2% year over year, below the expected 2.3% and the prior reading of 2.6%. On a month-over-month basis, it increased 0.1%, also below both the expectation and the prior reading of 0.2%. Excluding food and energy, core PPI rose 2.4% year over year, below the expected 2.6% and the prior 3.0%; on a month-over-month basis it was flat, the mildest reading in nearly four months, and also better than the expected 0.2% rise. After the data was released, the U.S. dollar index fell in the short term, U.S. stock index futures rose, and risk appetite improved for a time.

In structural breakdown, service-sector costs fell 0.2% month over month, the first year-to-date decline, and also the largest month-on-month drop since March 2023. This was mainly related to lower profit margins among machinery and auto wholesalers. Goods prices, however, rose 0.6% month over month, the largest increase since February of this year. Among them, the energy demand index rose 1.9% month over month, with higher gasoline costs being an important driver. More importantly, the relatively stable indicator excluding food, energy, and trade rose 0.3% month over month, the largest increase in three months; year over year it rose to 3.3%, indicating that some sticky pressure has not completely disappeared. In other words, PPI growth is slowing while internal components are diverging at the same time: the services side is cooling more noticeably, while the goods side and parts of the core measures still show signs of back-and-forth.

Logically, the PPI measures prices at the production stage and provides some reference for subsequent terminal prices, but it is not one-to-one. Falling service costs helps reinforce the narrative that “inflation pressure is easing”; meanwhile, an energy and goods rebound, along with strength in indicators excluding trade, reminds the market that the deceleration slope may not be smooth. Therefore, pricing in trading usually does not rest on a single indicator; instead, it cross-validates PPI with the forthcoming CPI, labor market and income data, and officials’ remarks within the same framework. Regarding the September policy path, there remains disagreement in the market over the size of rate cuts, with discussions of both 25 basis points and 50 basis points; uncertainty itself also tends to raise volatility.

For the impact on the crypto market, the path is mainly not “a single level directly determines the coin price,” but indirect effects through three channels: expectations for dollar liquidity, the imagination space for real interest rates, and global risk appetite. If inflation data continues to point to cooling, market pricing of a policy shift may strengthen, improving the overall environment for high-volatility risk assets. If subsequent data shows reversals, expectation adjustments could also bring pullbacks. Assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are sensitive to macro narratives, but during data-heavy periods, the common quick switch between “trading expectations” and “trading facts” can easily amplify short-term volatility.

The editor’s view is: this time, the PPI undershot expectations with a larger-than-expected slowdown, strengthening the evidence chain that upstream price pressures are easing and making rate-cut discussions receive more attention. However, the rebound on the goods side and the rise in some core indicators suggest that the process of inflation cooling may still be bumpy. One should not extrapolate a single PPI print into a trend endgame, nor should it be simplified into a one-way trading signal. Going forward, it is important to focus on the breadth and stickiness of CPI, the pace of cooling in the labor market, and whether policy communication aligns with the data. Understanding single-month data within a fuller macro sequence is more helpful for grasping the medium-term environment for risk assets than chasing sentiment.

美国7月PPI同比降至2.2%核心环比持平

美国劳工部门公布的最新生产者价格数据显示，7月PPI整体弱于市场预期，上游通胀压力继续缓和。市场将其视为观察美联储政策路径的重要线索之一，并迅速把关注点转向后续更具权重的消费者价格数据。

核心事实方面，7月PPI同比上涨2.2%，低于预期的2.3%和前值2.6%；环比上涨0.1%，同样低于预期与前值的0.2%。剔除食品和能源后的核心PPI同比上涨2.4%，低于预期2.6%和前值3.0%；环比持平，为近四个月最温和读数，也好于预期的0.2%涨幅。数据公布后，美元指数短线走低，美股期货走高，风险偏好一度改善。

从结构拆解看，服务业成本环比下降0.2%，为年内首次下滑，也是2023年3月以来最大单月降幅，主要与机械和汽车批发商利润率回落有关。商品价格则环比上涨0.6%，为今年2月以来最大升幅，其中需求能源指数环比上升1.9%，汽油成本走高是重要推动。更需留意的是，剔除食品、能源和贸易后的相对稳定指标环比上升0.3%，为三个月来最大涨幅，同比升至3.3%，说明部分粘性压力并未完全消失。换言之，整体PPI放缓与内部结构分化同时存在：服务端降温更明显，商品端与部分核心度量仍有反复迹象。

逻辑上，PPI衡量的是生产环节价格，对后续终端物价具有一定传导参考意义，但并非一一对应。服务成本回落有助于强化“通胀压力缓解”的叙事；而能源和商品反弹、以及剔除贸易后的指标走强，则提醒市场降温斜率可能并不平滑。正因如此，交易定价往往不会停留在单一指标，而会把PPI与即将公布的CPI、就业与收入、以及官员表态放在同一框架中交叉验证。关于9月政策路径，市场对降息幅度仍存分歧，25个基点与50个基点的讨论同时存在，不确定性本身也会抬升波动。

对加密市场的影响路径，主要不是“某个点位直接决定币价”，而是通过美元流动性预期、实际利率想象空间和全球风险偏好三条链条间接作用。若通胀数据持续指向降温，市场对政策转向的定价可能增强，从而改善高波动风险资产的整体环境；若后续数据出现反复，预期修正也可能带来回撤。比特币、以太坊等资产对宏观叙事敏感，但在数据密集期，常见“预期交易”与“事实交易”的快速切换，短线波动容易放大。

编辑判断是：本次PPI超预期放缓，强化了上游价格压力减轻的证据链，也让降息讨论更受关注；但商品端反弹与部分核心指标回升表明，通胀回落进程仍可能波折。不宜把单次PPI外推为趋势终局，更不宜把它简化成单向交易信号。后续应重点跟踪CPI的广度与粘性、劳动力市场降温节奏，以及政策沟通是否与数据同步。把单月数据放入更完整的宏观序列里理解，比追逐情绪更有助于把握风险资产的中期环境。

The reason I entered—if I said it out loud, it would be embarrassing.

Not because I’d researched it thoroughly.

Because I saw other people posting screenshots of their profits, and I couldn’t help myself.

Because I lost money earlier this morning, and I was unwilling to accept it.

And another trade—purely because I was bored.

I kept staring at the chart until late at night, feeling like if I didn’t do something, I’d itch to trade.

Those reasons are far more humiliating than any technical indicators.

But writing them down actually loosened the tightness in my chest.

Honest record-making may not make you money immediately, but it can keep lies from sounding so righteous.

With $MMT’s drop today, it’s basically asking everyone who came in: Why did you enter back then?

If you can’t answer, then losing isn’t unfair.

ETH is now around 1889. I’ll state my conclusion first: the information flow is hottest, while the funding flow is coldest. At this level, I’ll continue to observe.

These past two days, the news is genuinely strong. ETFs have seen net inflows for 7 consecutive trading days, and there’s even a proposal to add staking into the ETF. Sentiment jumped straight to 7.4. KOLs are calling for longs everywhere. But when you look at the spot order book: in the past 3 hours, there have been 12 fifteen-minute candles, and not a single one turned red on the funds. Large orders have net flowed out by nearly 270,000. In active trades, buy orders don’t even make up half. The louder the calls, the more decisively the money leaves.

Price action is equally tangled. For 7 days, price has been stuck in the box between 1852 and 1943. MACD is still below the zero line, and ADX is only 17—this is a typical range-bound, non-trending consolidation. But the 50-day line beneath provides support, and the MFI is at 61, still a fairly mild buy signal. In the order book, the buy wall’s thickness is more than 5 times that of the sell. If price really drops, there are people underneath ready to catch it.

The big players are giving a de-risking signal: the long/short position ratio has fallen by more than 2 percentage points over the past 7 hours, and the long share has come back to around 57%. The good news is that contract OI is shrinking, and the funding rate is hovering right at the floor (0.0085%), with no overcrowding risk on the long side.

So the issue isn’t whether ETH is good or bad—it’s that both longs and shorts are waiting for the other side to move first. The direction suggested by the news is completely opposite to where the money is going. This kind of split is the easiest setup for both sides to get slapped. My approach: don’t chase longs and don’t chase shorts. Let price choose its direction—break above 1943 on volume before discussing longs; drop below 1872 before discussing the risk. For now, I’m watching.

title: Crypto Market Update: Bitcoin Holds Near $63K as ETF Outflows and SEC Rulemaking Shape Sentiment
subTitle:
Bitcoin opened the new KST day with a cautious market tone, trading near the $63,000 area while Ethereum stayed below the $1,900 level. Economic Times reported that softer U.S. inflation did not deliver a strong relief rally, with traders still focused on broader risk conditions and the Federal Reserve's next signals. That keeps crypto in a familiar macro-driven range rather than a clean trend.

ETF flows are now a key short-term pressure point. CoinStats' latest update showed U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF flows flipped negative on August 12, with about $61.1 million in net outflows. The move was led by redemptions from FBTC and IBIT, although the seven-day total remained positive. This is not a full institutional reversal, but it does interrupt the bid that had helped stabilize Bitcoin and Ether during recent sessions.

Regulation is also moving back to the front page. Bitcoin.com News reported that the SEC and CFTC are advancing their own crypto paths while the CLARITY Act waits for a September procedural vote. The SEC is expected to consider a new framework for digital asset offerings on August 14, potentially giving crypto startups a more tailored way to raise capital. Markets may treat this as a signal that U.S. rulemaking is moving even if Congress remains slow.

Tokenization remains the longer-term institutional theme. Investor's Business Daily highlighted growing interest from major financial platforms in tokenized stocks, bonds and real-world assets, while noting that regulation and investor protection remain unresolved.

For traders, the practical takeaway is patience. ETF outflows can cap rallies, but policy progress and tokenization headlines support the structural story. Until Bitcoin clears its range with volume, ETH and major altcoins may stay headline-sensitive and prone to fast rotations. #BTC #ETH #Crypto #ETF #Macro

ETH is around 1894 now; sentiment is lit, but the money isn’t keeping up.

The news flow is warm all around: ETF net inflows, ETF staking applications—these headlines are everywhere. KOL sentiment is split into 7.5, and “bullish” posts over the last 24 hours are three times the “bearish” ones. With this kind of heat, prices would have already pushed higher in other times—but in reality, over the past 24 hours it has only risen by a fraction, and 1900 still isn’t being held.

The problem is where the money comes from. Over the last few hours, spot large orders are seeing net outflows of nearly 70,000 ETH. Over the past ~12 consecutive 3-hour funding candles, not a single one is positive—real capital has been draining out. On the other side, on-chain leverage borrowing has surged more than tenfold over 12 hours. Most of the buying inside the market is borrowed, not genuine spot capital.

Positions are also crowded. Whale accounts are long by more than 60%, and the overall accounts are long by about 70%. But over these past few hours, whale long positions have actually been decreasing. Price is grinding just below the 1-day high, and the 4-hour structure is still pointing downward.

In plain terms, this is a divergence: hot sentiment, cold capital. The news is lifting attention, but the money that determines price is withdrawing. Any rebound propped up by leverage usually has limited follow-through, and volatility can easily get amplified.

At this level, I’m not chasing longs. If you already have positions, watch the 1880 zone; if it breaks, don’t stubbornly hold. If you’re in cash, wait for capital to flow back and for price to hold above 1900 before reassessing. Chasing in right now doesn’t offer a great risk-reward.

Last night I stared at the contract order book. The moment a trade just appeared as executed, a friend asked, “Shouldn’t it be settled now?” I didn’t reply—but in my mind jumped the one thing about DuskEVM that’s easiest to confuse: trading being ordered and packaged is not the same as when assets truly gain underlying finality. They’re not the same step.

@Dusk_Foundation  Instead of cramming all functions into a single chain, it separates execution from settlement. A Solidity transaction first goes into the DuskEVM sorter, where it’s included in an L2 block; then the batcher publishes the transaction data to DuskDS. State commitments are connected to underlying settlement via fault proofs. The earlier part is about speed, while the later part is about verifiability—so cross-layer transfers can’t rely on “waiting a few seconds” to guess finality. You must read the protocol state. This is especially critical for securities: execution receipts can appear quickly, but the equity, bond, and payment legs can’t rely on probabilistic confirmation.

Under DuskDS runs Succinct Attestation. Each round: a block is proposed by a random provisioner, verified by one committee, and then ratified by another committee; after approval, it achieves deterministic finality. For applications that use the Ethereum toolchain and need to go through DuskEVM, you connect directly to L1 assets, follow the Phoenix private transaction model, and the logic that uses ZK primitives—then you go with Rust/WASM on DuskVM.$DUSK  It’s also used for execution gas, settlement, and staking security.#dusk  Where the real weight lies is separating “seeing the trade executed quickly” from “definitely owning the asset,” and then reconnecting them using the same verifiable settlement.

Last night I didn’t rush to look at the K-line charts. Instead, I split a small amount of DUSK into two transfers: one went via Moonlight, and the other via Phoenix. The most direct feedback isn’t that “privacy is more advanced,” but that the same settlement layer provides two different data boundaries. Moonlight uses a public account model: balances, the sender, and the amounts are visible. Phoenix represents funds as encrypted notes, and uses zero-knowledge proofs to confirm that inputs are valid, the amount is conserved, and there’s no double-spending—while not revealing the specific amounts or the relationship between notes.

This is what I think Dusk is most worth watching: it doesn’t turn privacy into a blindfold everyone has to swallow. Instead, it makes public and confidential transactions into a native model where you can choose. Security tokens can’t broadcast all business positions to the whole network, and they also can’t rely on regulators and auditors just taking one sentence—“trust me.” Phoenix’s viewing keys and selective disclosure exactly separate “not visible to the public” from “verifiable by authorized parties.”

The real experience also exposes the costs. Privacy notes require the wallet to scan, manage, and generate proofs; the interaction is heavier than a normal transfer. Having two models coexist also means wallets need to clearly explain balance types, receiving addresses, and failure reasons—otherwise users will only reach a plain conclusion: the coin is still there, but I panicked first.

So I won’t automatically give a high score just because of the four words “privacy RWA.” What truly needs to be validated is whether Dusk Trade can turn identity eligibility, restricted transfers, asset legs, and payment legs settlement into a continuous process—rather than forcing users to manually piece together the protocols. <@Dusk_Foundation > is a valid technical direction, but the product closed loop still needs real-asset and ongoing-transaction testing. <$DUSK > <#dusk > <#BTC #ETH >

Print the document in the morning: the computer first pops up “Sent,” but the printer only spits out the paper a few seconds later. When I first got started with DuskEVM, I ran into a similar illusion too—just because the browser has seen the transaction doesn’t mean the underlying settlement has already completed.

I connected to Chain ID 745, used a separate test account to bridge test funds to the EVM side, and then deployed a Counter contract with Foundry. Following the transaction onward, I think @Dusk_Foundation  isn’t really about “compatibility with another EVM,” but about whether, after execution and settlement are separated, the application can correctly recognize the state.

First, the transaction is handed to the DuskEVM sequencer and enters an L2 block; then the batcher publishes the data to DuskDS. The state commitments and fault proofs carry the execution result down into the underlying settlement. So “quickly recorded” and “finally posted” are two different things. If you only look at block time for asset issuance or cross-layer transfers, you might mistake something that hasn’t settled yet for something irreversible.

The advantage is very practical: developers keep the Solidity toolchain; $DUSK  handles EVM gas and the flow between L1 and the EVM; DuskDS is responsible for data availability and settlement. But the cost can’t be ignored either: with an extra sequencer, batcher, and bridge, you add another set of runtime and failure risks. My focus isn’t whether the contract can be deployed, but whether the product can clearly show “packaged, published, settled.” The biggest fear in financial on-chain systems isn’t being slow by a few seconds—it’s mistaking half-completed for completed. #dusk  #BTC #ETH

title: Sending Bitcoin to Binance vs. Sending Bitcoin to a Web3 Wallet
subTitle:
When you send Bitcoin, it is easy to think that you are simply moving coins from one wallet to another. Technically, that is not quite what happens.
Bitcoin exists on the Bitcoin blockchain as transaction outputs called UTXOs (Unspent Transaction Outputs). Your wallet does not physically contain the Bitcoin. Your wallet holds the keys that allow you to control Bitcoin associated with your addresses.
That distinction becomes extremely important when you send Bitcoin to a cryptocurrency exchange such as Binance instead of sending it to a self-custody Web3 wallet.
1. Sending Bitcoin to Binance
When you want to deposit BTC into Binance, Binance gives you a Bitcoin deposit address associated with your Binance account.
You copy that address and send BTC from your external wallet or another service to it.
The Bitcoin transaction itself takes place on the Bitcoin blockchain. Binance does not make the Bitcoin transaction happen; the Bitcoin network does.
The transaction contains inputs, outputs, amounts and other information. Once broadcast, it is identified by a transaction ID (TXID). The Bitcoin blockchain records the transaction and its outputs.
After the transaction receives the required confirmations, Binance identifies the incoming transaction and credits your Binance account.
Binance's current guidance says that when making a crypto deposit, the selected network must match the network from which you are sending. Binance also notes that a deposit may require a tag, memo or payment ID for some assets.
The important difference
When you send BTC to Binance, you are sending Bitcoin to an address controlled by Binance, not to a private wallet for which you personally hold the private key.
Binance is a custodial service. The exchange controls the private keys associated with its infrastructure and maintains an internal record of which Binance customer is entitled to the assets.
This means that after Binance credits your deposit, the amount you see in your Binance account is not necessarily sitting as an individual, untouched transaction output belonging exclusively to your particular deposit address.
The exchange manages its cryptocurrency holdings and customer balances through its own infrastructure.
This is fundamentally different from a self-custody wallet.
2. Sending Bitcoin to a Web3 or Self-Custody Wallet
A self-custody wallet works differently.
Examples include wallets where you control your own recovery phrase or private keys.
The wallet application is essentially an interface that allows you to view blockchain information and use your private keys to authorize transactions.
The Bitcoin remains on the blockchain.
Your wallet does not contain a pile of Bitcoin inside your phone.
Instead, the wallet controls the keys necessary to spend Bitcoin associated with your addresses.
If someone sends BTC to your Bitcoin address, the transaction becomes part of the Bitcoin blockchain.
If the output remains unspent, it is a UTXO associated with that address.
If you later spend it, your wallet creates a new Bitcoin transaction using that UTXO as an input.
3. What You Can See on the Blockchain
Bitcoin's blockchain is public.
A blockchain explorer can show information such as:
the Bitcoin address;incoming transactions;outgoing transactions;transaction IDs;amounts;confirmations;block information;and whether particular outputs have subsequently been spent.
Bitcoin transactions are permanently recorded in the blockchain once confirmed. Bitcoin's documentation explains that transactions are chained together and that outputs can subsequently be spent only once.
Therefore, if BTC was genuinely sent to a particular Bitcoin address, there should be a blockchain transaction associated with that address.
4. Why Binance Can Look Different From a Web3 Wallet
Suppose you send 0.01 BTC to your own self-custody wallet.
The blockchain records the transaction to your address.
Your wallet reads that blockchain information and displays your balance.
Now suppose you send 0.01 BTC to your Binance deposit address.
The blockchain records the transaction to the Binance-controlled address.
After Binance recognizes and confirms the deposit, Binance credits your account internally.
The exchange's internal accounting is therefore an additional layer between you and the blockchain.
This is why your Binance balance and the balance visible for a particular blockchain address should not automatically be interpreted as exactly the same thing.
5. What Happens When You Withdraw BTC From Binance
The process is essentially reversed.
You enter an external Bitcoin address as the withdrawal destination.
Binance processes the withdrawal and broadcasts a Bitcoin transaction.
Once the transaction is on the blockchain, it has a TXID.
You can use that TXID to investigate the transaction on a Bitcoin blockchain explorer.
The Bitcoin then becomes associated with an output controlled by the destination address.
If the destination is your own self-custody wallet, your wallet should eventually recognize the incoming transaction.
6. Confirmations Matter
A Bitcoin transaction can initially be broadcast without being confirmed in a block.
As miners include transactions in blocks, confirmations accumulate.
More confirmations provide increasing assurance that the transaction is part of the established blockchain history. Bitcoin's developer documentation explains the relationship between confirmations and transaction finality.
This is why an exchange may wait for a certain number of confirmations before crediting a deposit.
The exact requirements can vary by asset, network and exchange policy.
7. The Network Must Match
One of the most important rules in cryptocurrency is:
The sending network and receiving network must be compatible.
This is especially important with assets that can exist on multiple networks.
Binance specifically warns that selecting the wrong network can result in funds not being credited or potentially being permanently lost.
Bitcoin itself should be sent over the Bitcoin network when making a standard BTC deposit.
Do not assume that an address is safe simply because it looks similar to another cryptocurrency address.
8. What If Binance Says the Deposit Never Arrived?
Do not immediately conclude that the Bitcoin disappeared.
Start with the transaction itself
Find the TXID and determine:
Does the transaction actually exist?Is it a Bitcoin transaction?Is it confirmed?What address received the BTC?How much BTC was sent?Has the receiving output subsequently been spent?Was the destination address actually the Binance deposit address?Was the correct network used?Did Binance require additional information for that particular deposit?
Binance's own guidance says that a missing crypto deposit can require information such as the TXID, amount and sender's address when using its recovery process.
9. The Most Important Lesson
There is a major difference between:
"The blockchain says the BTC was sent to my Binance deposit address."
and
"Binance says my account was credited with the BTC."
The first is a blockchain fact.
The second is an exchange-accounting fact.
You need to establish both when investigating a missing deposit.
If the blockchain shows that the BTC was successfully sent to the correct Binance deposit address, but Binance did not credit the account, that is a very different problem from a situation in which the alleged transaction does not exist on the Bitcoin blockchain.
10. Never Confuse a Wallet Address With a Wallet Account
A Bitcoin address is not the same thing as a Binance account.
Likewise, a wallet application is not the blockchain itself.
The blockchain contains the transaction history.
The wallet software gives you an interface for interacting with that blockchain.
An exchange provides an account interface and maintains custody and internal accounting for customer assets.
Understanding these three layers—blockchain, wallet, and exchange—makes missing-crypto investigations much easier.
Final takeaway
When sending BTC, always record:
the cryptocurrency;the network;the destination address;the amount;the date and time;and especially the TXID.
Those details allow you to distinguish between a transaction that was never broadcast, a transaction that is still unconfirmed, a transaction sent to the wrong address, a transaction sent using the wrong network, and a legitimate blockchain deposit that an exchange has not credited.
For significant amounts, never rely solely on a screenshot saying "successful." Verify the transaction independently on the appropriate blockchain.

After trading for ten years, the biggest takeaway wasn’t how many times I caught opportunities with big upside—it was learning to give up decisively when I’m wrong.

Many people hold on to positions stubbornly, because they can’t accept losing. But the market won’t feel sorry for you just because you’re down—it will simply keep moving in its own rhythm. Holding on for a trade might save you 5% in losses, but it might also wipe out your entire principal.

This ETH move is the best example. After breaking above the previous high, it retested—seemingly a chance to short, but in reality it was the main players washing the market. If you didn’t set a stop loss in advance, you’re likely to be swept out near the lowest point, then watch helplessly as the price keeps rising.

My principle now is very simple: set a stop loss before entering. When it’s hit, cut it—no hesitation, no excuses. After cutting, look for the next opportunity. The market is never short of opportunities; what it lacks is your principal.

Trading isn’t gambling—it’s a probability game. Staying alive matters more than winning. #交易 #ETH

Honestly, I’m getting less and less interested in watching one or two short-term points. Sitting in front of the chart all day is exhausting—mentally draining, and the profits don’t even make up for the hair you lose from staying up late. Right now, BTC has been hovering around 63k, ETH is hanging around 1.88k, and SOL has at least shown a bit of strength today, up about +1%. Instead of guessing whether tomorrow will go up or down, think about what, exactly, you’re making money from.

My framework has three rules:

First, don’t always try to sell at the very top when it comes to spot. With big coins like BTC, the real profit is holding; if you can’t hold, then it’s just a number game. My approach is to buy in batches—add another tranche when it dips to the right level, then reduce in portions as it rises. You always keep inventory in hand and also keep cash ready.

Second, with contracts: I advise you not to treat them as your main play. Funding fees, slippage, liquidation levels—none of them is anything other than eating into your principal. If you really want to play, use small size, low leverage, and set stop losses. Use it as a hedging tool, not something you can rely on to turn things around.

Third, position size matters more than entry price. Even if your judgment is spot-on, if your position is wrong, it’s still going to be painful. When weekend liquidity tightens, the market can easily be swept away by a single needle-like move. So at times like this, I’m used to lowering leverage and keeping a base position—holding the risk in your own hands.

To be honest, the end of trading isn’t prediction—it’s discipline. Are your main holdings right now spot or contracts? How many tenths or what percentage is usually your position size? Let’s talk.

So what does this mean in practice? It points to institutions quietly positioning themselves—not retail trying to bottom-fish. Goldman Sachs acquired NEOS for $2.25 billion, and Fidelity plans to add staking functionality to its Ethereum ETF. These are all mainstream players moving in. They’re not here to trade short-term swings; they’re here to lock in positions for the long term and earn yield.

Does the business logic hold up? Yes. Between Ethereum staking annualized returns and ETF management fees, this setup provides institutions with a steady cash-flow stream. Bitmine’s $257 million in annualized staking income is a good example.

From the cycles I’ve personally run through, whenever the market is at its most panicked, it’s often “smart money” that’s accumulating. Of course, I’m not a god—whether ETH can really rebound next week still depends on whether volume can pick up. If $1,825 holds, then there’s a chance; if it breaks, then we’ll have to see.

My view this week hasn’t changed—I still believe in ETH’s fundamentals. It’s just that I’m even more certain now that institutional moves are happening faster than I expected.

What do you think about this round of institutional positioning—can ETH hold up? Or does the entry of big institutions actually create an opportunity for retail to bail?

【ETH筑底ing，还是下跌中继？】

一周前ETH还在1930美元晃悠，现在1870美元附近打转，一个月前那是2100美元。算下来7天跌了1%，一个月跌了将近11%。

但有意思的来了——恐惧贪婪指数这周均值只有29，市场怕得要死。偏偏ETH在这位置稳住了，没继续往下砸。成交量低得可怜，说明卖的人也在观望。

这件事落到实处意味着什么？机构在悄悄布局，不是散户在抄底。Goldman Sachs22.5亿美元收购NEOS，Fidelity要给以太坊ETF加上质押功能，这些都是传统金融的正规军在进场。他们不是来炒短差的，是来长期锁仓收利息的。

商业逻辑通不通？通。ETH年化质押收益加上ETF管理费，这套玩法对机构来说就是稳稳的现金流。Bitmine那2.57亿美元年化质押收入就是例子。

从我自己跑过的周期看，每次市场最恐慌的时候，往往是聪明钱在吸筹。当然，我不是神仙，下周能不能真的起来还看成交量能不能放大。1825美元撑住就有戏，跌破的话那另说。

这一周我的看法没变过——我还是相信ETH的基本面，只是比上周更确认了机构的动作比我想的快。

The third time, my confidence exploded.

title: ETH Faces $846 Million Short Liquidations Above $1,968, Coinglass Says
subTitle:
Ethereum is sitting on a powder keg of short positions. According to the latest data from Coinglass, if ETH breaks above $1,968, the cumulative short liquidation intensity across major centralized exchanges will reach approximately $846 million. That figure represents one of the more significant near-term liquidation clusters currently visible on the Ethereum futures market and has quickly drawn attention from traders watching for a potential short squeeze.
The setup is straightforward yet powerful. #ETH   #Ethereum  #Crypt #Liquidations   ##USJulyCPI&PPIDueThisWeek CryptoMarket Large numbers of leveraged traders have positioned themselves short around and above current price levels. As price approaches $1,968, those positions face mounting pressure. A decisive move through that level would force exchanges to automatically close out underwater short accounts, creating a cascade of market buy orders. Those forced buys can accelerate the upward move, liquidating even more shorts in a self-reinforcing loop commonly known as a short squeeze.
Liquidation maps from Coinglass function as heatmaps of leverage risk. They aggregate open interest across major exchanges and estimate the dollar value of positions that would be forcibly closed at specific price thresholds. The $846 million short liquidation cluster above $1,968 stands out because it is both sizable and relatively close to current trading levels. In recent sessions ETH has been hovering in the $1,880–$1,900 range, meaning the distance to the key trigger is not extreme. A modest bullish impulse or a wave of covering could be enough to test the level.
This kind of positioning imbalance does not guarantee an immediate breakout. Markets can grind sideways or reverse before reaching high-liquidity clusters. However, the presence of such a large short overhang creates asymmetric risk. On the upside, a push through $1,968 could unlock significant forced buying. On the downside, Coinglass data also shows that a drop below roughly $1,788 would trigger around $727 million in long liquidations. The market therefore sits between two meaningful liquidity pools, with the short side currently more concentrated just overhead.
The broader context adds weight to the data. Ethereum has spent recent weeks consolidating after a period of weakness, tracking broader crypto market sentiment that has been dominated by Bitcoin’s own technical struggles. Funding rates on ETH perpetual futures have fluctuated, at times turning negative as shorts paid to maintain their positions. Open interest remains elevated relative to some quieter periods earlier in the year, indicating that leveraged traders have not fully exited the market. When open interest stays high and price compresses near a major liquidation cluster, the conditions for a sharp directional move improve.
A short squeeze of this magnitude would not necessarily mark the start of a sustained bull market. It could simply be a violent, short-lived liquidation event that clears overleveraged positions before price settles into a new range. Historical examples in both Bitcoin and Ethereum show that large liquidation cascades often produce rapid candles followed by periods of digestion. Still, the mechanical effect is real: every short that gets liquidated becomes a market buy, and $846 million in concentrated short risk is enough to move price meaningfully in a market that has shown sensitivity to leverage flows.
Traders monitoring the situation are watching several confirmation signals. A clean break and hold above $1,968 on rising volume would increase the probability of cascading liquidations. Failure to reclaim the level, or a sharp rejection, would leave the short cluster intact and potentially shift focus back toward the long liquidation zone lower down. Exchange-specific data also matters; the largest concentrations of short leverage often sit on Binance, OKX, and Bybit, meaning activity on those platforms can amplify or dampen the effect.
Coinglass’s liquidation estimates are not precise predictions of exact dollar flows. They are modeled intensities based on open interest and estimated leverage at different price bands. Actual liquidations can be higher or lower depending on how positions are distributed, how quickly price moves, and whether traders add or reduce risk in real time. Nevertheless, the $846 million figure provides a clear, data-driven reason why many market participants are treating $1,968 as a critical near-term level for Ethereum.
In a market still recovering from broader risk-off pressure, the existence of this short liquidation wall offers both opportunity and danger. For bulls, it represents potential fuel. For bears, it is a level that must be defended or risk forced covering. Either way, the Coinglass data has put $1,968 firmly on the radar. If Ethereum can push through it with momentum, the $846 million short liquidation cluster will no longer be theoretical—it will become live market activity.
